breakfast.name: Bougatsa (Custard-Filled Phyllo Pastry)
ingredients: Powdered sugar and cinnamon for dusting
instructions: Heat milk in a saucepan until it just begins to simmer — do not boil
Whisk semolina into the hot milk gradually, stirring constantly to prevent lumps
Add sugar and stir until the mixture thickens into a smooth custard, about 5 minutes
Remove from heat, let cool slightly, then whisk in eggs one at a time and vanilla
Brush a baking dish with melted butter, layer 6-8 sheets of phyllo, brushing each with butter
Pour the custard filling over the phyllo base, spreading evenly
Layer 6-8 more phyllo sheets on top, buttering each one generously
Score the top layers into squares or rectangles with a sharp knife
Bake at 180°C for 35-40 minutes until the phyllo is deeply golden and shattering
Dust generously with powdered sugar and cinnamon — serve warm, never cold
breakfast.description: The iconic breakfast of Thessaloniki — flaky, shatteringly crisp phyllo wrapped around a silky semolina custard, dusted with powdered sugar and cinnamon. Bougatsa shops open at dawn and the sight of a bougatsa master stretching paper-thin dough by hand is one of the most filmed food moments in Greece. The cross-section reveal — golden layers over creamy custard — goes viral every time.

breakfast.name: Strapatsada (Greek Scrambled Eggs with Tomato)
ingredients: 3 ripe tomatoes, grated on a box grater
Salt and freshly ground black pepper
instructions: Grate the tomatoes on the large holes of a box grater, discarding the skins
Heat olive oil in a skillet over medium heat
Add the grated tomato pulp and cook until reduced by half, about 8 minutes
Season with oregano, salt, and pepper
Crack eggs directly into the tomato, stir gently to create large, soft curds
Cook just until the eggs are barely set — they should still be creamy
Transfer to a plate, crumble feta generously over the top
Serve immediately with thick slices of crusty bread for scooping
breakfast.description: The Greek answer to Turkish menemen and Middle Eastern shakshouka — eggs scrambled into a concentrated, sweet tomato sauce made by grating fresh tomatoes on a box grater. The grating technique (discard the skin, keep the pulp) is a Greek kitchen hack that has gone massively viral. Topped with crumbled feta and scooped with bread, this is island breakfast perfection.

breakfast.name: Tiropita (Greek Cheese Pie)
instructions: Combine crumbled feta, ricotta, eggs, dill, and pepper in a bowl — do not add salt, feta provides enough
Mix until well combined but still slightly chunky — you want pockets of cheese
Brush a baking dish with melted butter
Layer 6-7 sheets of phyllo, brushing each generously with melted butter
Spread the cheese filling evenly over the phyllo base
Layer 6-7 more sheets on top, brushing each with butter
Tuck the edges under to seal, brush the top with remaining butter
Score the top into squares or diamonds with a sharp knife
Sprinkle a few drops of water on top to help the phyllo crisp without curling
Bake at 180°C for 30-35 minutes until golden and puffed
breakfast.description: Greece's most beloved savory pie — layers of crispy, buttered phyllo encasing a tangy filling of feta and soft cheese with fresh dill. Found at every bakery, kafeneio, and yia-yia's kitchen across the country. The triangular hand-pie version is the quintessential Greek street food, and the sound of biting through those shattering phyllo layers is ASMR gold.

breakfast.name: Spanakopita (Spinach and Feta Phyllo Pie)
ingredients: 500g fresh spinach, washed and roughly chopped
instructions: Wilt spinach in a large pan, then squeeze out every drop of moisture — this is critical or the pie will be soggy
Sauté onion and spring onions in olive oil until soft
Combine spinach, onions, crumbled feta, eggs, dill, salt, and pepper
Brush a baking dish with melted butter, layer 7-8 sheets of phyllo, buttering each
Spread the spinach-feta filling in an even layer
Top with 7-8 more buttered phyllo sheets
Score the top layers into portions
Bake at 180°C for 35-40 minutes until deeply golden and crisp
Let rest 10 minutes before cutting — the filling needs to set
The phyllo should shatter when you cut it — if it bends, it needed more butter or more time
breakfast.description: The spinach and feta pie that conquered the world — spanakopita is perhaps the single most recognized Greek dish globally. Layers of butter-brushed phyllo wrapped around earthy spinach, tangy feta, and aromatic dill. The triangle-fold hand-pie version is a street food icon, and the full tray version feeds every Greek Easter table. Trending perpetually as the ultimate savory pastry.

breakfast.name: Greek Yogurt with Honey and Walnuts
ingredients: 60g walnuts, lightly toasted and roughly chopped
instructions: Spoon thick Greek yogurt into bowls — it should be dense enough to hold a spoon upright
Drizzle generously with Greek thyme honey — the floral, herbal flavor is irreplaceable
Scatter toasted walnuts over the top
Sprinkle with sesame seeds and a whisper of cinnamon
Add fresh figs when in season — halved, they make this bowl impossibly photogenic
Serve immediately — this is the Greek breakfast that launched a global health food trend
breakfast.description: The dish that made Greek yogurt a global phenomenon — thick, strained yogurt drizzled with floral thyme honey and topped with crunchy walnuts. This simple combination is responsible for a multi-billion dollar yogurt industry outside Greece. The honey-drizzle moment and the creamy spoonful are among the most replicated food videos. Greece's gift to the modern breakfast table.

lunch.name: Souvlaki (Grilled Meat Skewers in Pita)
ingredients: 600g pork shoulder or chicken thigh, cut into 2cm cubes
Sliced tomato, red onion, and parsley for serving
instructions: Marinate meat cubes in olive oil, lemon juice, garlic, oregano, salt, and pepper for at least 30 minutes (overnight is better)
Thread marinated meat onto skewers — not too tightly, leave small gaps for even cooking
Grill over high heat or charcoal, turning every 2-3 minutes, until charred and cooked through
Warm pita breads on the grill for 30 seconds per side
Slide meat off skewers onto warm pita
Top with tomato, red onion, a handful of parsley, and a generous dollop of tzatziki
Wrap tightly — the proper wrap technique uses parchment paper so you can eat it walking
In Greece, pork is the traditional meat — chicken souvlaki is the tourist version (both are good)
lunch.description: Greece's most iconic street food — cubes of marinated pork or chicken grilled over charcoal, wrapped in warm pita with tzatziki, tomato, and onion. Every Greek city has its legendary souvlaki joint, and the debate over the best one is a national sport. The sizzling grill, the wrap technique, and the first bite are endlessly viral. Pork is traditional — chicken is fine, but pork is the real deal.

lunch.name: Gyros (Rotisserie Meat in Pita)
ingredients: Greek pita breads, tzatziki, tomato, onion, and fries for serving
instructions: Slice pork shoulder as thinly as possible — almost shaved
Marinate in olive oil, vinegar, garlic, cumin, paprika, oregano, salt, and pepper for at least 2 hours
For home cooking: layer marinated slices flat in a deep roasting pan, pressing down firmly
Roast at 200°C for 60-70 minutes until the edges are deeply caramelized and crispy
Shave or slice the roasted meat thinly from the edges — the crispy bits are the prize
Warm pita breads, spread with tzatziki
Layer sliced gyros meat, add tomato, onion, and the essential: French fries inside the wrap
Yes, fries go inside the gyros — this is non-negotiable in Greece
Wrap tightly in paper, eat immediately while the fries are still hot
lunch.description: The spinning cone of seasoned meat that hypnotizes everyone who walks past — gyros is Greece's contribution to the world's most satisfying street food. Thinly shaved from a vertical rotisserie, stuffed into pita with tzatziki, tomato, onion, and (crucially) French fries inside the wrap. The vertical spit carving videos are mesmerizing, and the fries-inside-the-wrap revelation goes viral constantly.

lunch.name: Horiatiki (Classic Greek Village Salad)
ingredients: 4 large ripe tomatoes, cut into irregular chunks
1 large cucumber, peeled and thickly sliced
1 green bell pepper, sliced into rings
1 red onion, thinly sliced into rings
200g block of feta cheese (one whole slab)
Extra virgin olive oil, generous pour
instructions: Cut tomatoes into large, irregular chunks — never dice them small
Peel cucumber and cut into thick half-moons — never thin slices
Slice green pepper into rings, red onion into thin rings
Arrange vegetables on a platter — do not toss, just pile them naturally
Place one thick slab of feta on top — never crumble it, the whole block sitting on top is the signature
Scatter Kalamata olives around the feta
Drizzle very generously with the best extra virgin olive oil you have
Sprinkle dried oregano and salt over the feta and vegetables
There is no lettuce in a real horiatiki — this is non-negotiable
Serve with crusty bread to soak up the olive oil and tomato juices at the bottom
lunch.description: The original Greek salad — and the source of infinite arguments about what does and does not belong in it. No lettuce. No vinegar. No fancy dressing. Just peak-season tomatoes, cucumber, pepper, onion, a whole slab of feta on top (never crumbled), Kalamata olives, and a drowning of olive oil. The slab-of-feta-on-top moment is one of the most photographed dishes in the Mediterranean.

lunch.name: Fasolada (Greek White Bean Soup)
ingredients: 400g dried white beans (gigantes or cannellini), soaked overnight
Red wine vinegar and olive oil for serving
instructions: Drain soaked beans, cover with fresh water, bring to a boil, and cook 10 minutes — drain again
In a large pot, heat olive oil and sauté onion, carrot, and celery until softened
Add drained beans, crushed tomatoes, bay leaves, paprika, salt, and pepper
Add enough water to cover beans by about 3cm
Bring to a boil, then reduce to a gentle simmer
Cook for 75-90 minutes until beans are completely tender and creamy — add water if needed
The broth should be thick and silky — not watery soup but not paste either
Serve in deep bowls, drizzled with raw extra virgin olive oil and a splash of red wine vinegar
Eat with crusty bread and olives — this is the unofficial national dish of Greece
lunch.description: Greece's unofficial national dish — a humble, soul-warming white bean soup that Greeks consider more important than moussaka. Slow-simmered beans in tomato with carrots, celery, and a generous pour of olive oil. Fasolada is the dish that sustained Greece through centuries of fasting, poverty, and celebration alike. Trending as part of the Mediterranean diet movement and Blue Zone longevity research.

lunch.name: Gemista (Stuffed Tomatoes and Peppers)
instructions: Cut tops off tomatoes and peppers, carefully hollow out the insides — save the tomato pulp
Blend or grate the tomato pulp into a puree
Mix rice with grated onion, mint, parsley, half the olive oil, tomato puree, salt, and pepper
Fill each tomato and pepper about three-quarters full — the rice expands significantly
Replace the tops as lids
Arrange stuffed vegetables snugly in a baking dish
Tuck potato wedges between the vegetables — they roast in the juices and become incredible
Drizzle remaining olive oil over everything, add a cup of water to the dish
Bake at 180°C for 70-75 minutes until rice is cooked and vegetables are collapsed and caramelized
Serve at room temperature — gemista are best slightly cooled, never straight from the oven
lunch.description: The iconic Greek summer dish — ripe tomatoes and peppers stuffed with herbed rice, baked until collapsed and caramelized, with potato wedges roasting in the juices below. Gemista is the taste of a Greek grandmother's kitchen, and the sight of a tray fresh from the oven — jewel-toned, fragrant, and glistening — is pure food photography magic. The potatoes that absorb all those juices are the secret star.

lunch.name: Dolmades (Stuffed Grape Vine Leaves)
ingredients: 40-50 grape vine leaves (jarred or fresh, blanched)
instructions: If using jarred vine leaves, rinse well and blanch briefly — if fresh, blanch in boiling water 2 minutes
Sauté onion and spring onions in olive oil until soft
Mix rice with sautéed onions, dill, mint, half the lemon juice, salt, and pepper
Place a vine leaf shiny side down, add a teaspoon of filling near the stem end
Fold stem end over filling, fold in the sides, then roll into a tight little cigar
Pack dolmades seam-side down in a pot, arranging them in tight concentric circles
Place a plate on top to weigh them down (this prevents unrolling during cooking)
Add remaining lemon juice, olive oil, and enough water to just cover
Simmer on low heat for 45-50 minutes until rice is tender and leaves are silky
Serve at room temperature with thick Greek yogurt or avgolemono sauce
lunch.description: Tiny packages of herbed rice wrapped in tender grape vine leaves — dolmades are one of the oldest dishes in the Mediterranean, and the rolling technique videos are hypnotically viral. The patience required to stuff fifty little parcels is part of the ritual, usually done as a family activity. The meatless version with rice, dill, and mint served cold is the summer standard across every Greek island.

dinner.name: Moussaka (Layered Eggplant and Meat Bake)
instructions: Salt eggplant slices and let drain for 30 minutes — this removes bitterness and excess moisture
Brush eggplant with olive oil and roast at 200°C until golden on both sides, about 20 minutes
Brown ground meat with onion and garlic, add tomatoes, cinnamon, salt, and pepper — simmer 20 minutes
Make béchamel: melt butter, whisk in flour, gradually add milk while stirring constantly
Cook béchamel until thick, remove from heat, stir in egg yolks and half the cheese
Layer roasted eggplant in a deep baking dish as the base
Spread meat sauce evenly over the eggplant
Add another layer of eggplant on top of the meat
Pour béchamel over everything, spreading to cover completely — sprinkle remaining cheese
Bake at 180°C for 45-50 minutes until golden and bubbling — let rest 20 minutes before cutting
dinner.description: The Greek national dish that rivals lasagna for layered-bake supremacy — silky roasted eggplant, spiced meat sauce with a whisper of cinnamon, and a golden béchamel crown. Moussaka is Greece's most famous export and the cross-section when you cut into a properly rested moussaka — showing those distinct, perfect layers — is one of the most viral food moments in Mediterranean cuisine. The cinnamon in the meat is the secret.

dinner.name: Pastitsio (Greek Baked Pasta)
instructions: Cook pasta until just al dente — it will cook more in the oven
Brown ground meat with onion, add crushed tomatoes, cinnamon, allspice, salt, and pepper — simmer 20 minutes
Make béchamel: melt butter, whisk in flour, gradually add milk, cook until thick
Remove béchamel from heat, stir in eggs and half the grated cheese
Toss cooked pasta with a little of the béchamel to coat
Layer half the pasta in a deep baking dish
Spread meat sauce evenly over the pasta layer
Top with remaining pasta
Pour béchamel generously over the top, sprinkle with remaining cheese
Bake at 180°C for 45-50 minutes until golden on top — rest 20 minutes before cutting into squares
dinner.description: Greece's answer to lasagna — layers of tubular pasta, cinnamon-spiced meat sauce, and a thick golden béchamel top. Pastitsio is the dish every Greek grandmother makes for Sunday lunch, and cutting into the baked slab to reveal those perfect layers of pasta, meat, and cream is deeply satisfying. The warming spices — cinnamon and allspice in the meat — give it a distinctly Greek character that sets it apart from Italian baked pastas.

dinner.name: Kleftiko (Slow-Roasted Lamb in Parchment)
ingredients: 1.5kg bone-in lamb shoulder, cut into large chunks
Parchment paper and kitchen twine or foil for sealing
instructions: Make small incisions all over the lamb and insert garlic slivers deep into the meat
Rub lamb with lemon juice, olive oil, oregano, salt, and pepper
Place lamb and potatoes on large sheets of parchment paper (or foil)
Tuck sliced tomatoes and feta around and on top of the lamb
Seal the parchment into tight parcels — no steam should escape
Place parcels on a baking tray and roast at 160°C for 3.5-4 hours
The lamb should be falling off the bone, the potatoes melting, the feta dissolved into the sauce
Open parcels at the table — the aromatic steam burst is theatrical and irresistible
The name means 'stolen meat' — bandits cooked lamb in sealed underground pits to hide the smoke
dinner.description: Literally 'stolen meat' — named after Greek mountain bandits who slow-cooked lamb in sealed pits to hide the smoke from Ottoman soldiers. The lamb roasts in its own sealed parchment for hours until it falls off the bone, the potatoes melt into the juices, and the feta becomes the sauce. Opening the parchment at the table releases a cloud of aromatic steam that is pure culinary theatre. The origin story alone makes this go viral.

dinner.name: Stifado (Greek Beef and Onion Stew)
ingredients: 1kg beef chuck, cut into large cubes
700g small pearl onions or shallots, peeled
instructions: Brown beef cubes in olive oil in batches — do not crowd the pan, you need deep color
Remove beef, add whole pearl onions and cook until just starting to color
Deglaze with red wine, scraping up all the fond from the bottom
Return beef to the pot, add crushed tomatoes, vinegar, garlic, bay leaves, cinnamon, cloves, and allspice
Add enough water to barely cover the meat
Bring to a boil, then reduce to the gentlest simmer — use a diffuser if needed
Cook for 2-2.5 hours until beef is fork-tender and the sauce is thick and glossy
Do not stir — gently shake the pot occasionally to prevent sticking
The onions should be whole, sweet, and melting — if they break apart, you stirred too much
Serve with crusty bread or orzo pasta — the sauce is the treasure
dinner.description: A deeply warming beef stew where the onions outnumber the meat and the spicing is pure Greek — cinnamon, cloves, allspice, and a splash of red wine vinegar that cuts through the richness. Stifado is peasant food elevated to art, simmered for hours until the beef dissolves and the whole pearl onions become sweet, silky gems. The sweet-spice aroma that fills the house while it cooks is unforgettable.

dinner.name: Saganaki (Flaming Fried Cheese)
ingredients: 250g kefalograviera, kasseri, or halloumi cheese, cut into 1cm thick slabs
instructions: Cut cheese into slabs about 1cm thick and the size of your palm
Briefly dip cheese in water, then dredge lightly in flour — the water helps the flour stick
Heat olive oil or butter in a small, heavy skillet until very hot
Fry cheese until deeply golden and crusty on the bottom, about 2 minutes
Flip and fry the other side until golden — the inside should be melted but not running
Optional: pour brandy or ouzo over the hot cheese and carefully ignite — shout 'OPA!'
Squeeze lemon juice over the cheese immediately to extinguish and add brightness
Serve in the hot pan with crusty bread — eat immediately while still molten inside
dinner.description: The most theatrical appetizer in Greek cuisine — a thick slab of cheese fried until golden, then doused with brandy and set on fire while everyone at the table shouts 'OPA!' The flaming cheese ritual is one of the most filmed restaurant moments worldwide. Even without the fire, the sizzling pan of golden, crispy-outside-molten-inside cheese with a squeeze of lemon is irresistible. Simple, dramatic, viral.

dinner.name: Grilled Octopus with Vinaigrette
instructions: Simmer octopus in a covered pot with no added water — it will cook in its own liquid — for 45-50 minutes until tender
Test tenderness with a knife — it should slide in easily
Drain and let cool slightly, then cut into pieces
Brush pieces generously with olive oil
Grill over very high heat for 2-3 minutes per side until charred and the tentacle tips are crispy
Whisk olive oil, red wine vinegar, oregano, and lemon juice into a vinaigrette
Arrange grilled octopus on a platter, drizzle with vinaigrette
Scatter capers, olives, and parsley over the top
The charred tentacle tips curling on the grill is one of the most beautiful sights in Greek cooking
dinner.description: Octopus hung on a line to dry in the Aegean sun, then grilled over charcoal until the tentacles char and curl — this image IS Greek island cuisine. The combination of tender, smoky octopus with sharp vinaigrette, capers, and oregano is pure Mediterranean perfection. Photos of octopus drying on clotheslines against whitewashed walls and blue sea are among the most iconic food images in the world.

snacks.name: Tzatziki (Yogurt, Cucumber, and Garlic Dip)
ingredients: 1 large cucumber, grated and squeezed dry
3 cloves garlic, minced or grated on a microplane
1 tbsp red wine vinegar or lemon juice
instructions: Grate cucumber on the large holes of a box grater
Place grated cucumber in a clean towel and squeeze out every drop of liquid — this is the most important step
Combine drained cucumber with thick yogurt
Add minced garlic — start with 2 cloves if you are cautious, but 3 is the Greek way
Stir in olive oil, vinegar or lemon juice, dill, and salt
Refrigerate for at least 1 hour to let flavors meld — overnight is ideal
Drizzle with olive oil before serving
Serve with warm pita, as a souvlaki accompaniment, or as a dip for everything
snacks.description: The dip that conquered the world — cool, tangy yogurt loaded with garlic and cucumber, drizzled with olive oil. Tzatziki is the essential companion to souvlaki and gyros, but it has become a global dip phenomenon in its own right. The key secret: squeeze every drop of water from the cucumber, or you will have soup instead of dip. This one technique tip has been shared millions of times.

snacks.name: Koulouri Thessalonikis (Sesame Bread Ring)
ingredients: Honey water (2 tbsp honey dissolved in 100ml warm water) for dipping
instructions: Mix flour, yeast, salt, and sugar — add warm water and olive oil, knead for 10 minutes until smooth and elastic
Let dough rise for 1 hour until doubled
Divide dough into 8 equal pieces
Roll each piece into a long rope about 40cm long
Twist the rope and form into a ring, pressing ends together firmly
Dip each ring into honey water, then roll in sesame seeds, pressing to coat thickly
Place on a baking sheet and let rise 20 more minutes
Bake at 200°C for 18-20 minutes until deeply golden and the sesame seeds are toasted
The crust should be crunchy, the inside soft and slightly chewy — if it is hard, it overbaked
snacks.description: The iconic sesame-crusted bread ring sold from street carts across Greece — the most popular street snack in the country. Every morning in Thessaloniki and Athens, vendors sell koulouri from carts for less than a euro, and the sight of golden rings stacked on sticks is quintessentially Greek. Crunchy sesame crust, soft chewy inside, eaten walking to work with a Greek coffee. Street food at its simplest and best.

snacks.name: Fava (Yellow Split Pea Puree from Santorini)
ingredients: 300g yellow split peas (Santorini fava if available)
1 red onion, thinly sliced, for garnish
instructions: Rinse split peas and place in a pot with the chopped onion, garlic, and water to cover by 5cm
Bring to a boil, skim any foam that rises
Reduce heat and simmer for 40-45 minutes until split peas are completely falling apart
Drain most of the cooking liquid (save it), then mash or blend until silky smooth
Add half the olive oil, lemon juice, salt, and pepper — add back cooking liquid if too thick
Spread on a platter in a smooth layer
Garnish with thinly sliced raw red onion, capers, and a generous drizzle of olive oil
Serve at room temperature with crusty bread — this is Santorini's most famous dish
snacks.description: Santorini's signature dish — silky, golden split pea puree drizzled with olive oil and topped with raw red onion and capers. Despite the name, Greek fava is not made from fava beans but from yellow split peas that grow in Santorini's volcanic soil, giving them a unique sweet, mineral flavor. This simple, elegant dish trending as the poster child of Santorini's culinary scene and the Mediterranean plant-based movement.

snacks.name: Kolokithokeftedes (Zucchini Fritters)
instructions: Grate zucchini and salt generously — let sit 10 minutes, then squeeze out all moisture in a towel
Combine squeezed zucchini with crumbled feta, spring onions, mint, dill, egg, flour, and pepper
The mixture should hold together when pressed — add a little more flour if needed
Heat olive oil in a skillet — about 1cm deep, not deep-frying
Drop spoonfuls of the mixture into the hot oil, flatten slightly
Fry 3-4 minutes per side until deeply golden and crispy
Drain on paper towels
Serve hot with tzatziki on the side — they are best within 10 minutes of frying
snacks.description: Crispy, herby zucchini fritters loaded with feta, mint, and dill — the quintessential Cretan appetizer that appears on every Greek island taverna menu in summer. The trick is squeezing every drop of moisture from the grated zucchini, or they steam instead of crisp. Golden, crunchy outside, tender and herb-packed inside, served with a bowl of cold tzatziki. Trending as a plant-forward Mediterranean snack.

snacks.name: Dakos (Cretan Barley Rusk Salad)
ingredients: 4 ripe tomatoes, grated on a box grater
Extra virgin olive oil, generous pour
instructions: Briefly dip each rusk under running water — just enough to soften the surface, not soak through
Place rusks on a platter
Grate tomatoes on the large holes of a box grater, discarding skins — spread pulp over each rusk
Crumble soft myzithra or ricotta generously over the tomatoes
Add a few Kalamata olives to each rusk
Drizzle very generously with extra virgin olive oil
Sprinkle with dried oregano and sea salt
Serve immediately before the rusks absorb too much liquid and turn to mush
snacks.description: Crete's answer to bruschetta — a crunchy barley rusk moistened with grated tomato, piled with creamy myzithra cheese, olives, and a river of olive oil. Dakos is the simplest and most ancient Cretan dish, and its photogenic, rustic beauty against a backdrop of whitewashed Cretan walls makes it massively shareable on social media. The grated-tomato technique has gone viral as a Greek cooking hack.

desserts.name: Baklava (Walnut and Honey Phyllo Pastry)
instructions: Mix chopped walnuts with cinnamon and cloves
Brush a baking dish with melted butter, layer 8 sheets of phyllo, brushing each with butter
Spread a thin layer of the nut mixture over the phyllo
Add 3-4 more buttered phyllo sheets, then another nut layer — repeat until nuts are used
Top with 8 final sheets of phyllo, each brushed with butter
Using a very sharp knife, cut into diamonds before baking — this is essential
Bake at 170°C for 45-50 minutes until deeply golden and the layers are visible at the edges
While baking, make syrup: boil sugar, water, honey, lemon peel, and cinnamon stick for 10 minutes
Pour hot syrup over hot baklava — you will hear it sizzle and absorb
Let soak for at least 4 hours, preferably overnight — patience is everything
desserts.description: The queen of Mediterranean pastries — layers upon layers of butter-brushed phyllo encasing spiced walnuts, soaked in a honey-lemon syrup that penetrates every crevice. Greek baklava uses honey and walnuts (Turkish uses pistachios and sugar syrup), and the Greek version's floral, complex sweetness has its own devoted following. The syrup-pouring moment — hot syrup hitting hot baklava with an audible sizzle — is one of the most satisfying sounds in food.

desserts.name: Galaktoboureko (Custard-Filled Phyllo with Syrup)
ingredients: 300g sugar, 200ml water, juice of half a lemon (for syrup)
instructions: Heat milk until simmering, gradually whisk in semolina — stir constantly until thick, about 5 minutes
Remove from heat, stir in 200g sugar, lemon zest, and vanilla
Let cool slightly, then whisk in eggs one at a time
Brush a baking dish with melted butter, layer 10 sheets of phyllo, buttering each generously
Pour the warm custard over the phyllo base
Layer 10 more sheets of phyllo on top, buttering each one
Tuck edges under, brush top with remaining butter
Score into squares or diamonds
Bake at 180°C for 40-45 minutes until deeply golden
Make syrup: boil sugar, water, and lemon juice for 8 minutes — pour hot syrup over hot galaktoboureko
desserts.description: Greece's most decadent dessert — a thick, creamy semolina custard sandwiched between shattering layers of butter-soaked phyllo, drenched in lemon-scented syrup. Galaktoboureko is what baklava dreams of being — richer, creamier, more indulgent. The contrast between the crisp, syrup-soaked phyllo and the silky custard center is texturally extraordinary. Every Greek bakery's version is slightly different, and the debates are fierce.

desserts.name: Loukoumades (Greek Honey Doughnuts)
instructions: Mix flour, yeast, sugar, and salt — add warm water and stir into a thick, sticky batter
Cover and let rise for 1 hour until doubled and bubbly
Heat oil for deep frying to 180°C
Dip two spoons in water, take a small ball of batter with one spoon, use the other to push it into the hot oil
Fry in batches until deeply golden and puffed, turning once — about 3-4 minutes total
Drain briefly on paper towels
Pile onto a platter, drizzle generously with warm honey
Sprinkle with cinnamon and crushed walnuts
Serve immediately — loukoumades must be eaten hot, they do not keep
desserts.description: Golden, puffy fried dough balls drenched in warm honey and sprinkled with cinnamon and walnuts — Greece's original doughnut, older than civilization itself (they were served at the ancient Olympics). The honey-drizzle moment over a steaming pile of loukoumades is peak food content. Modern Greek shops have gone viral adding Nutella, ice cream, and Lotus Biscoff, but the classic honey version is untouchable.

desserts.name: Portokalopita (Greek Orange Phyllo Cake)
ingredients: 10 sheets phyllo dough, crumpled and dried overnight
300g sugar, 300ml orange juice, 1 cinnamon stick (for syrup)
instructions: Crumple phyllo sheets loosely and leave out overnight to dry — or bake briefly at low heat until dry and crisp
Whisk eggs with sugar until thick and pale
Add yogurt, olive oil, orange juice, orange zest, baking powder, and vanilla
Tear the dried phyllo into rough pieces and fold into the wet mixture
Let sit 10 minutes until phyllo absorbs the liquid — the batter will look shaggy and uneven
Pour into a buttered baking dish
Bake at 180°C for 40-45 minutes until golden and set in the center
Make orange syrup: boil sugar, orange juice, and cinnamon stick for 10 minutes
Pour hot syrup over hot cake — let it soak for at least 1 hour
Serve at room temperature — the texture should be moist, custardy, with crispy phyllo edges
desserts.description: A magical Greek cake made from torn, dried phyllo dough soaked in an orange-scented batter and drenched in orange syrup — the phyllo creates an otherworldly texture that is neither cake nor pastry but something entirely unique. Portokalopita has gone massively viral as people discover this trick of using stale phyllo as a cake ingredient. The no-flour concept and the unusual texture revelation make this one of the most shared Greek recipes online.

desserts.name: Rizogalo (Greek Rice Pudding)
instructions: Rinse rice and cook in 300ml water until water is absorbed and rice is half-cooked
Add milk, sugar, and lemon peel to the rice
Cook on medium-low heat, stirring frequently, for 25-30 minutes until thick and creamy
The rice should be completely tender and the consistency like thick porridge
Remove lemon peel, stir in vanilla
For a richer version: temper egg yolks with a little hot rice mixture, then stir back in
Pour into individual bowls or glasses
Let cool to room temperature, then refrigerate until set
Dust generously with cinnamon before serving — the cinnamon pattern on top is the signature
desserts.description: Greece's ultimate comfort dessert — slow-cooked rice in creamy milk, scented with lemon peel and vanilla, served cold with a thick dusting of cinnamon on top. Every Greek kafeneio and taverna has its own version, and the simplicity is the point. Rizogalo is the dessert that Greek grandmothers make when nothing else will do — warm, nurturing, and perfect. The cinnamon-dust pattern on top is the finishing touch.

drinks.name: Frappé and Freddo (Greek Iced Coffees)
ingredients: 2 tsp instant coffee (for frappé) or 1 double espresso shot (for freddo)
2 tsp sugar (adjust to taste — vary: sketos/no sugar, metrios/medium, glykos/sweet)
A cocktail shaker or hand frother
instructions: For Frappé: place instant coffee, sugar, and 2 tbsp cold water in a shaker or tall glass
Shake vigorously or blend with a hand frother until a thick, light-brown foam forms — this foam is everything
Pour over ice in a tall glass, add cold water, and optionally a splash of milk
For Freddo Espresso: pull a double espresso shot, add sugar while hot, pour into a shaker with ice
Shake hard until frothy and ice-cold, pour into a glass over fresh ice
For Freddo Cappuccino: make freddo espresso, then froth cold milk separately and spoon on top
Sip slowly through a straw — both drinks are meant to last an hour at a café table
The frappé was invented in Thessaloniki in 1957 by accident — it is Greece's national drink
drinks.description: The drinks that define Greek café culture — the frappé (invented in 1957 when a Nescafé rep could not find hot water at a trade fair) is instant coffee shaken into a thick foam over ice, sipped for hours at a seaside table. The freddo espresso and freddo cappuccino are the modern evolution — shaken espresso over ice with cold milk foam. Greek iced coffee culture predates the global iced coffee trend by decades, and the café-by-the-sea frappé moment is one of the most iconic Greek images.

drinks.name: Ellinikos Kafes (Greek Coffee)
ingredients: 2 heaping tsp very finely ground coffee (Turkish/Greek grind — like powder)
Sugar to taste (sketos/none, metrios/1 tsp, glykos/2 tsp per cup)
A small glass of cold water (served alongside, the traditional accompaniment)
instructions: Measure cold water using the demitasse cup — one cup of water per serving
Pour water into the briki, add coffee and sugar
Stir only once to combine — do not stir again after this point
Place briki on the lowest possible heat
Watch carefully — the coffee will slowly form a dark foam (kaimaki) on the surface
As the foam rises to the rim, remove from heat immediately — do not let it boil over
Pour slowly into cups, distributing the foam (kaimaki) equally — this foam is the mark of quality
Let grounds settle for 1 minute before sipping — never drink the muddy bottom
Turn the cup upside down on the saucer when finished — the grounds tell your fortune
drinks.description: The original coffee ritual — powdery-fine coffee brewed slowly in a small brass briki until a thick foam (kaimaki) rises to the rim. Greek coffee is served in tiny cups, sipped slowly, and when you finish, you flip the cup and read your fortune in the grounds. The fortune-telling ritual (tasseography) has fascinated the internet, and the careful, meditative brewing process is endlessly watchable. Do not call it Turkish coffee in Greece.

drinks.name: Rakomelo (Warm Honey Raki)
instructions: Pour raki into a small saucepan
Add honey, cinnamon stick, cloves, orange peel, and star anise
Heat gently on low — never let it boil or the alcohol will burn off
Stir until honey dissolves completely into the spirit
Let simmer on the lowest heat for 5-8 minutes to infuse the spices
Strain into small glasses or shot glasses
Serve warm — rakomelo is a winter drink, served after dinner or at celebrations
In Crete, raki is offered free at the end of every meal — rakomelo is the festive version
drinks.description: Cretan grape spirit warmed with honey, cinnamon, and cloves — Greece's answer to mulled wine, served in small glasses after dinner on cold nights. In Crete, raki (tsikoudia) is offered free at the end of every taverna meal, and the honey-spiced version is the celebratory upgrade. The warm, honeyed, spiced aroma fills the room, and the ritual of sharing tiny glasses of rakomelo after a feast is the essence of Cretan hospitality. Trending as a cozy winter cocktail.
